name: Nigel Richards
one_line: World Scrabble champion in three languages, exactly one of which he speaks.

facts.claim: won the French-language World Scrabble Championship in 2015 and again in 2018 without speaking French
facts.note: Confirmed by every outlet covering it (CBC, NPR, Euronews). At the 2015 ceremony in Louvain he received a standing ovation and needed a translator to say thank you.

facts.claim: memorized the French Scrabble dictionary - roughly 400,000 words - in nine weeks
facts.note: ESPN: 'mastered the French scrabble dictionary or roughly 400,000 words in nine weeks' time.' Wikipedia says 'two months of studying the French lexicon' - same window, phrase as 'nine weeks' or 'about two months'. Liz Fagerlund (ex-president, NZ Scrabble Association): 'He doesn't speak French at all, he just learnt the words.'
Plus 5x US National, 10x UK Open, 12x Singapore Open, 15x King's Cup (Bangkok). ESPN (written 2018) says four world titles because the fifth came in 2019.

facts.claim: won the Spanish-language world championship in 2024, his first Spanish competition, taking 23 of 24 games - without speaking Spanish
facts.note: Also confirmed by VOA and Euronews (which says he studied Spanish word lists for about a year for this one). Born 1967, so 57 years old at the 2024 win.

facts.claim: compiled the first two perfect scores ever recorded at the Spanish world championship
facts.note: In a language he does not speak, in his first attempt.

facts.claim: introduced to Scrabble by his mother at age 28; she reportedly told him he would not be good at it because he could not spell
facts.note: ESPN confirms the introduction at 28. The mother's line ('you won't do good in this game... you can't spell very well') is widely reported but secondhand - use reported speech, never a direct quote. Her name: Adrienne Fischer.

facts.claim: refuses interviews - turns down requests with a smile and walks away; has essentially never explained his method
facts.note: ESPN verbatim: 'He turns down interview requests with a crack of a smile and walks away.'

facts.claim: cycled 14 hours from Dunedin to Christchurch through bad weather to his first national championship in 1998 - then cycled back
facts.note: Texture fact. Gilad cut it from the script as irrelevant - keep for long-form.

facts.claim: after winning everything in English he took up French Scrabble as a new challenge in 2015
facts.note: QZ/CBC framing: 'took up the challenge' of the French championship. Fagerlund on his method: 'he doesn't even study the pages word by word. He can look at a page full of words and absorb them all.'

facts.claim: analysts ran 919 of his endgame moves (more than nine hundred, across 588 games) through Quackle, the standard Scrabble analysis engine: Richards made 11 errors (1.2% error rate); the computer made four times as many errors and lost seven times as many points
facts.note: Analysis by Francis Desjardins and Gilles Blanchette. Defector verbatim: 'Quackle made four times as many errors and lost seven times as many points as Nigel.' Phrase the engine as 'a top Scrabble computer' - Quackle is the best-known analyzer, not provably the strongest.

facts.claim: outscores opponents by 72 points per game; the world's second-best player, David Eldar (2023 world champion), outscores his by 49
facts.note: Defector: 'Eldar has outscored his opponents by a whopping 49 points per game. Nigel has outscored his opponents by 72 points per game.'

facts.claim: world champion in three languages - English, French, Spanish - and speaks one of them
facts.note: Derived directly from the title list. Do NOT claim 'nobody else has won two' - plausible but unsourced.

comparison.gap_description:
World champion
in 3 languages.
Speaks 1 of them.

story_beat: His mother taught him Scrabble at 28, reportedly telling him he wouldn't be any good because he couldn't spell. He went on to memorize the French dictionary - about 400,000 words - in nine weeks, win the French world title, and thank the audience through a translator.
